summary: This note traces early American automobile manufacturing from the 1890s into the early 1900s. It highlights the Duryea brothers' Duryea Motor Wagon Company as the first American automobile manufacturer, the Autocar Company as the oldest surviving US motor vehicle maker, and Ransom E. Olds's Oldsmobile as dominant in the era. It also describes the Thomas B. Jeffery Company's Rambler, the second mass-produced automobile, and the rapid growth of Cadillac, Winton, and Ford within a year.
one_line: Early American automobile makers from the 1890s to about 1902, including Duryea, Autocar, Oldsmobile, Rambler, Cadillac, Winton and Ford.
key_facts: Charles and Frank Duryea founded the Duryea Motor Wagon Company in 1893.
The Duryea Motor Wagon Company was the first American automobile manufacturing company.
The Autocar Company was founded in 1897.
The Autocar Company remains the oldest operating motor vehicle manufacturer in the United States.
Ransom E. Olds founded the Olds Motor Vehicle Company, later known as Oldsmobile.
The Olds Motor Vehicle Company's production line was running in 1901.
The Thomas B. Jeffery Company developed the world's second mass-produced automobile.
The Thomas B. Jeffery Company built and sold 1,500 Ramblers in its first year.
The 1,500 Ramblers sold in the first year represented one-sixth of all existing motorcars in the United States at the time.
Cadillac was formed from the Henry Ford Company.
Within a year, Cadillac, Winton, and Ford were also producing cars in the thousands.
The note describes Ransom E. Olds and his Olds Motor Vehicle Company as dominating this era of automobile production.
